```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)

# Loads tidymodels, the shared constants and the business-impact helpers
# (section 11).
source("modeling_functions.R")

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

model_colour     <- "#4C6EF5"
benchmark_colour <- "#868E96"
```

# Introduction

The modeling notebook chose a final model on AUC. This notebook turns that
model into lending outcomes: how many applicants could be approved, and how
many of them would default, compared with a simpler way of ranking
applicants.

- **The model** is the final configuration from the modeling notebook: tuned
  XGBoost, no `CODE_GENDER`.
- **The benchmark** is `EXT_SOURCE_MEAN`, the average of the external credit
  scores (higher = safer). It stands in for underwriting on a bureau score
  alone.

Both are judged on **out-of-fold predictions**. Every training applicant is
scored by a model that never saw their outcome, so each prediction is an honest
estimate of how the model would score a new applicant.

# Final model setup

The final configuration is rebuilt from the modeling notebook's cached tuning,
re-scoring and tree-count results. Nothing below refits: every line printed
should say the result was loaded from the cache.

```{r load}
prepared <- load_prepared()
train    <- prepared$train
test     <- prepared$test

cv_metrics <- metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy)

compare_data  <- stratified_sample(train, prop = COMPARE_PROP)
compare_folds <- make_cv_folds(compare_data)
tune_data     <- stratified_sample(train, n = TUNE_N)
tune_folds    <- make_cv_folds(tune_data)
```

```{r final-config}
xgb_tune_wf <- workflow(build_recipe(tune_data), xgb_tune_spec())
xgb_grid    <- random_tune_grid(xgb_tune_wf, tune_data, size = 20)
xgb_tuning  <- tune_grid_cached("xgb_tuning", xgb_tune_wf, tune_folds,
                                xgb_grid, cv_metrics)

xgb_rescored <- rescore_top(xgb_tuning, xgb_tune_wf, compare_folds, cv_metrics, n = 3)
best_config  <- map(xgb_rescored, \(f) collect_metrics(f$result)) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = ".config") |>
  filter(.metric == "roc_auc") |>
  slice_max(mean, n = 1) |>
  pull(.config)
best_params <- show_best(xgb_tuning$result, metric = "roc_auc", n = 3) |>
  filter(.config == best_config) |>
  select(mtry:sample_size)

trees_sweep <- sweep_trees(extract_preprocessor(xgb_tune_wf), best_params,
                           trees = c(500, 1000, 1500, 2000),
                           folds = compare_folds, metrics = cv_metrics)
best_trees  <- pick_trees(trees_sweep)

final_exclude <- "CODE_GENDER"
final_wf <- finalize_workflow(
  workflow(build_recipe(train, exclude = final_exclude),
           xgb_tune_spec(trees = best_trees)),
  best_params)

final     <- fit_final_cached("xgb_tuned_final_nogender", final_wf, train)
final_fit <- final$result
```

The rebuilt configuration should match the saved final model exactly:

```{r config-check}
saved_args <- map(extract_spec_parsnip(final_fit)$args, rlang::eval_tidy)

config_check <- tibble(
  parameter = c(names(best_params), "trees"),
  rebuilt   = c(map_dbl(best_params, as.numeric), best_trees),
  saved     = map_dbl(parameter, \(p) as.numeric(saved_args[[p]]))
) |>
  mutate(match = rebuilt == saved)

stopifnot(all(config_check$match))
config_check |> kable(digits = 6)
```

# Out-of-fold predictions

All 307,511 training rows are split into 3 stratified folds with `pool = 0.05`,
as in the modeling notebook. Each fold is predicted by the final configuration
fit on the other two, so every applicant gets exactly one prediction from a
model that did not train on them. Only the predictions and per-fold metrics are
cached, to `data/cv_xgb_final_oof.rds`.

```{r oof}
full_folds <- make_cv_folds(train)

oof <- oof_predictions_cached("xgb_final_oof", final_wf, full_folds, cv_metrics)
```

The raw loan amount is read from the original CSV. The prepared data caps
`AMT_CREDIT` at the 99th percentile
(`r comma(prepared$params$money_caps[["AMT_CREDIT"]])`), which would understate
the credit held by the largest defaulted loans.

```{r scored}
prep_env  <- new.env()
source("data_preparation.R", local = prep_env)
raw_train <- prep_env$read_application("data/application_train.csv")
stopifnot(identical(raw_train$SK_ID_CURR, train$SK_ID_CURR))

scored <- oof$result$predictions |>
  arrange(.row) |>
  transmute(fold         = id,
            SK_ID_CURR   = train$SK_ID_CURR[.row],
            TARGET,
            default      = TARGET == "1",
            model_risk   = .pred_1,
            ext_source   = train$EXT_SOURCE_MEAN[.row],
            credit       = raw_train$AMT_CREDIT[.row])

n_applicants <- nrow(scored)
per_100k     <- 1e5 / n_applicants
```

Each fold should cover a third of the rows at the full default rate, every row
should be predicted once, and the mean predicted default should match the
actual rate in every fold:

```{r oof-check}
stopifnot(n_applicants == nrow(train),
          n_distinct(scored$SK_ID_CURR) == nrow(train),
          identical(scored$TARGET, train$TARGET))

oof_auc <- oof$result$per_fold |> filter(.metric == "roc_auc") |> select(fold = id, auc = .estimate)

scored |>
  group_by(fold) |>
  summarise(rows                   = n(),
            default_rate           = mean(default),
            mean_predicted_default = mean(model_risk),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(oof_auc, by = "fold") |>
  mutate(across(c(default_rate, mean_predicted_default), \(x) percent(x, accuracy = 0.01))) |>
  kable(digits = 4, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

Both scores ranked against the same outcomes, on all rows:

```{r auc}
score_auc <- tibble(
  score = c("Model (out-of-fold)", "Benchmark (EXT_SOURCE_MEAN)"),
  auc   = c(roc_auc_vec(scored$TARGET, scored$model_risk),
            roc_auc_vec(scored$TARGET, -scored$ext_source))
)
score_auc |> kable(digits = 4)
```

The out-of-fold AUC of
`r number(score_auc$auc[1], accuracy = 0.001)` is above the 0.748 measured on
the 20% comparison folds and close to the Kaggle private score (0.758): each
fold model here trains on 205,000 rows rather than 41,000. The benchmark's
`r number(score_auc$auc[2], accuracy = 0.001)` is the bar the model has to
clear to be worth more than the external scores alone.

`r comma(sum(duplicated(scored$ext_source) | duplicated(scored$ext_source, fromLast = TRUE)))`
applicants share an `EXT_SOURCE_MEAN` value with someone else, including
`r sum(train$EXT_SOURCE_COUNT == 0)` with no external score at all, who all
carry the imputed median. Ties are approved in row order.

# Approval tradeoff

Both scores rank every applicant from lowest to highest risk, and the
lowest-risk applicants are approved first. At each approval rate from 50% to
100%, the default rate among those approved:

```{r approval-paths}
model_path     <- approval_path(scored$model_risk, scored$default, scored$credit)
benchmark_path <- approval_path(-scored$ext_source, scored$default, scored$credit)

approval_rates <- seq(0.50, 1.00, by = 0.01)
curve_rows     <- round(approval_rates * n_applicants)

approval_curve <- bind_rows(
  Model     = model_path[curve_rows, ],
  Benchmark = benchmark_path[curve_rows, ],
  .id = "score") |>
  mutate(approval_rate = rep(approval_rates, 2),
         score         = factor(score, levels = c("Model", "Benchmark")))
```

```{r approval-chart}
#| fig-height: 5.5
# Direct labels at 60%: the model's below its line, the benchmark's above.
curve_labels <- approval_curve |>
  filter(approval_rate == 0.60) |>
  mutate(label = as.character(score),
         default_rate = default_rate + if_else(score == "Model", -0.004, 0.005))

ggplot(approval_curve, aes(approval_rate, default_rate, colour = score)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(scored$default), colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = curve_labels, aes(label = label),
            hjust = 0.5, size = 3.8, colour = "grey20", show.legend = FALSE) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = mean(scored$default), vjust = -0.5, hjust = 0,
           size = 3.4, colour = "grey45",
           label = paste("Approve everyone:", percent(mean(scored$default), accuracy = 0.01))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Model = model_colour, Benchmark = benchmark_colour),
                      labels = c("Model", "Benchmark (EXT_SOURCE_MEAN)")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1), breaks = seq(0.5, 1, 0.1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, NA),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(
    title    = "At every approval rate, the model's approved applicants default less",
    subtitle = "Default rate among approved applicants, approving the lowest-risk first",
    x = "Share of applicants approved",
    y = "Default rate among approved",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme(legend.position  = "top",
        legend.justification = "left",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

```{r approval-table}
approval_curve |>
  filter(approval_rate %in% seq(0.5, 1, by = 0.1)) |>
  select(score, approval_rate, default_rate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = score, values_from = default_rate) |>
  mutate(difference = Benchmark - Model,
         across(everything(), \(x) percent(x, accuracy = 0.01))) |>
  rename(model_default_rate = Model, benchmark_default_rate = Benchmark,
         benchmark_minus_model = difference) |>
  kable()
```

At 100% everyone is approved, so both curves meet at the overall default rate.
Below that, the gap is how much better the model separates risky applicants
from safe ones.

# Same risk, more approvals

A lender typically sets a risk appetite, a maximum default rate among approved
applicants, and approves as many applicants as it can within it. For each
target, each score approves the largest group of lowest-risk applicants whose
default rate stays at or under the target. The path is read one applicant at a
time, not in 1-point steps.

```{r targets}
targets <- c(0.04, 0.05, 0.06)

at_targets <- map(targets, \(t) {
  m <- at_target_rate(model_path, t)
  b <- at_target_rate(benchmark_path, t)
  same_size <- model_path[b$approved, ]   # the model at the benchmark's approval count
  tibble(
    target               = t,
    model_approval       = m$approval_rate,
    benchmark_approval   = b$approval_rate,
    model_cutoff         = sort(scored$model_risk)[m$approved],
    extra_approvals      = (m$approved - b$approved) * per_100k,
    extra_repay          = ((m$approved - m$defaults) - (b$approved - b$defaults)) * per_100k,
    extra_default        = (m$defaults - b$defaults) * per_100k,
    defaults_avoided     = (b$defaults - same_size$defaults) * per_100k,
    credit_avoided       = (b$defaulted_credit - same_size$defaulted_credit) * per_100k
  )
}) |>
  list_rbind()
```

**More approvals at the same default rate**, per 100,000 applicants:

```{r targets-approvals}
at_targets |>
  transmute(target_default_rate = percent(target, accuracy = 1),
            model_approval_rate     = percent(model_approval, accuracy = 0.1),
            benchmark_approval_rate = percent(benchmark_approval, accuracy = 0.1),
            extra_approvals = comma(extra_approvals),
            of_which_repay  = comma(extra_repay),
            of_which_default = comma(extra_default)) |>
  kable()
```

"Extra" is net: the model approves `extra_approvals` more applicants than the
benchmark in total, and `of_which_repay` is how many more repaying applicants
its approved group holds. The two groups differ in membership too, not just in
size; each score approves some applicants the other declines.

**Fewer defaults at the same approval rate.** Here the model approves exactly
as many applicants as the benchmark does at each target. The defaults it
avoids, and the loan amount (`AMT_CREDIT`, in the data's currency, not
converted) those defaulted loans carried, per 100,000 applicants:

```{r targets-avoided}
at_targets |>
  transmute(target_default_rate = percent(target, accuracy = 1),
            approval_rate       = percent(benchmark_approval, accuracy = 0.1),
            defaults_avoided    = comma(defaults_avoided),
            credit_of_avoided_defaults = comma(credit_avoided)) |>
  kable()
```

`credit_of_avoided_defaults` is the loan principal of those defaulted loans,
not the loss. The actual loss depends on how much was repaid before default and
what was recovered, neither of which is in the application data.

## Fold check

The figures above pool predictions from three fold models. Repeating the 5%
target within each fold separately shows whether the gain holds in every third
of the data, not just in the pooled ranking:

```{r targets-by-fold}
scored |>
  group_split(fold) |>
  map(\(d) {
    m <- at_target_rate(approval_path(d$model_risk, d$default, d$credit), 0.05)
    b <- at_target_rate(approval_path(-d$ext_source, d$default, d$credit), 0.05)
    tibble(fold                    = d$fold[1],
           model_approval_rate     = m$approval_rate,
           benchmark_approval_rate = b$approval_rate,
           extra_approvals_per_100k = (m$approved - b$approved) / nrow(d) * 1e5)
  }) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(across(ends_with("rate"), \(x) percent(x, accuracy = 0.1)),
         extra_approvals_per_100k = comma(extra_approvals_per_100k)) |>
  kable()
```

# Translating to Home Credit's financials

This section uses only the Q1 2019 figures from the Business Problem
Statement (BPS):

```{r financials}
q1_impairment_eur <- 430e6
q1_nii_eur        <- 889e6
loans_eur         <- 18755e6
cost_of_risk      <- 0.0229

bps_loss_reduction    <- 0.05   # BPS target: 5% fewer losses
bps_approval_gain_pts <- 1      # BPS target: +1 point approval rate

tibble(
  figure = c("Impairment losses, Q1 2019", "Net interest income, Q1 2019",
             "Loans to customers", "Cost of risk",
             "Check: impairment / loans to customers"),
  value  = c(sprintf("EUR %sM", comma(q1_impairment_eur / 1e6)),
             sprintf("EUR %sM", comma(q1_nii_eur / 1e6)),
             sprintf("EUR %sM", comma(loans_eur / 1e6)),
             percent(cost_of_risk, accuracy = 0.01),
             percent(q1_impairment_eur / loans_eur, accuracy = 0.01))
) |>
  kable()
```

The 2.29% cost of risk is one quarter's impairment over the loan book, so it is
a quarterly rate, and the basis-point changes below are on that basis.

## Relative reduction in defaults

At the 5% target, the benchmark approves
`r percent(at_targets$benchmark_approval[at_targets$target == 0.05], accuracy = 0.1)`
of applicants. The model approves the same number, and the reduction is the
defaults it avoids as a share of the defaults among the benchmark's approved
applicants, measured by count and by defaulted `AMT_CREDIT`:

```{r reduction}
bench_5 <- at_target_rate(benchmark_path, 0.05)
model_5 <- model_path[bench_5$approved, ]   # the model at the benchmark's approval count

reduction <- tibble(
  measure   = c("Default count", "Defaulted AMT_CREDIT"),
  benchmark = c(bench_5$defaults, bench_5$defaulted_credit),
  model     = c(model_5$defaults, model_5$defaulted_credit)
) |>
  mutate(avoided  = benchmark - model,
         relative_reduction = avoided / benchmark)

reduction |>
  mutate(across(c(benchmark, model, avoided), comma),
         relative_reduction = percent(relative_reduction, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(caption = sprintf("All %s training applicants; %s approved by each score",
                          comma(n_applicants), comma(bench_5$approved)))

count_reduction  <- reduction$relative_reduction[reduction$measure == "Default count"]
credit_reduction <- reduction$relative_reduction[reduction$measure == "Defaulted AMT_CREDIT"]
```

## Impairment and cost of risk

The `AMT_CREDIT`-based reduction is applied to impairment losses (annualised
as four times Q1) and to the cost of risk. Impairment is measured in money, so
the share of defaulted credit avoided is the closer match to it than the share
of defaults:

```{r impairment}
annual_impairment <- 4 * q1_impairment_eur

impact <- function(r) {
  tibble(loss_reduction         = r,
         annual_saving_eur      = annual_impairment * r,
         new_cost_of_risk       = cost_of_risk * (1 - r),
         cost_of_risk_change_bp = -cost_of_risk * r * 1e4)
}

impact(credit_reduction) |>
  transmute(loss_reduction         = percent(loss_reduction, accuracy = 0.1),
            annual_impairment      = sprintf("EUR %sM", comma(annual_impairment / 1e6)),
            annual_saving          = sprintf("EUR %sM", comma(annual_saving_eur / 1e6)),
            cost_of_risk           = percent(cost_of_risk, accuracy = 0.01),
            new_cost_of_risk       = percent(new_cost_of_risk, accuracy = 0.01),
            change_bp              = number(cost_of_risk_change_bp, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable()
```

Note: applying the count-based reduction
(`r percent(count_reduction, accuracy = 0.1)`) instead would give an annual
saving of EUR `r comma(impact(count_reduction)$annual_saving_eur / 1e6)`M and a
cost of risk of
`r percent(impact(count_reduction)$new_cost_of_risk, accuracy = 0.01)`
(`r number(impact(count_reduction)$cost_of_risk_change_bp, accuracy = 0.1)` bp).

## Scenarios

The conservative case is the BPS target, a 5% loss reduction. The upper bound
is the model's full reduction in defaulted `AMT_CREDIT` against the benchmark.
The last column is the
share of the model's edge over the benchmark that the conservative case needs.

```{r scenarios}
bind_rows(
  impact(bps_loss_reduction) |> mutate(scenario = "Conservative (BPS target)"),
  impact(credit_reduction)   |> mutate(scenario = "Upper bound (full reduction vs benchmark)")
) |>
  transmute(scenario,
            share_of_model_edge = percent(loss_reduction / credit_reduction, accuracy = 1),
            loss_reduction   = percent(loss_reduction, accuracy = 0.1),
            annual_saving    = sprintf("EUR %sM", comma(annual_saving_eur / 1e6)),
            new_cost_of_risk = percent(new_cost_of_risk, accuracy = 0.01),
            change_bp        = number(cost_of_risk_change_bp, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  relocate(share_of_model_edge, .after = last_col()) |>
  kable()
```

The conservative case needs
`r percent(bps_loss_reduction / credit_reduction, accuracy = 1)` of the
reduction the model shows against the benchmark.

Note: on the count-based reduction, the upper bound would be EUR
`r comma(impact(count_reduction)$annual_saving_eur / 1e6)`M a year, and the
conservative case would need
`r percent(bps_loss_reduction / count_reduction, accuracy = 1)` of the model's
edge.

## Approval rate

```{r approval-gain}
model_at_5 <- at_targets |> filter(target == 0.05)
approval_gain_pts <- (model_at_5$model_approval - model_at_5$benchmark_approval) * 100

tibble(
  measure = c("Model approval rate at 5% target", "Benchmark approval rate at 5% target",
              "Gain (percentage points)", "BPS target (percentage points)"),
  value   = c(percent(model_at_5$model_approval, accuracy = 0.1),
              percent(model_at_5$benchmark_approval, accuracy = 0.1),
              sprintf("+%.1f", approval_gain_pts),
              sprintf("+%.1f", bps_approval_gain_pts))
) |>
  kable()
```

## Assumptions

- **Losses scale with defaulted credit.** Impairment is assumed to fall in
  proportion to the `AMT_CREDIT` of defaulted loans
  (`r percent(credit_reduction, accuracy = 0.1)`; by count it is
  `r percent(count_reduction, accuracy = 0.1)`). Actual losses also depend on
  how much was repaid before default, recoveries and timing, which the data
  does not hold.
- **`TARGET` means payment difficulty**, not necessarily a loss: some flagged
  loans recover in full.
- **Per-100,000 results scale proportionally** to Home Credit's whole book,
  which assumes its applicants look like the training data.
- **The benchmark stands in for the current process.** Home Credit already
  uses machine learning in underwriting, so its current process is stronger
  than `EXT_SOURCE_MEAN` alone, and the upper bound overstates the gain.

# Personas

Two fictional applicants make the numbers concrete. Both start from the
**median applicant**: the median of every numeric application field and the
most common value of every categorical one, over all training applicants. Fields
missing for more than half of applicants (such as `EXT_SOURCE_1` and
`OWN_CAR_AGE`) are left missing, as they would be for a typical applicant. The
employment length median excludes the 365,243 placeholder. The personas pass
through the same `apply_prep()` as the real data, so every engineered feature
is consistent with the fields changed.

```{r median-applicant}
mode_of <- \(x) names(which.max(table(x)))

median_applicant <- raw_train |>
  select(-TARGET) |>
  mutate(DAYS_EMPLOYED = na_if(DAYS_EMPLOYED, 365243)) |>
  summarise(across(everything(), \(x)
    if (mean(is.na(x)) > 0.5) x[NA_integer_][1]
    else if (is.numeric(x)) median(x, na.rm = TRUE)
    else mode_of(x))) |>
  mutate(SK_ID_CURR = 0)
```

Each persona changes five things, all features the final model ranks highly:
the external scores (`EXT_SOURCE_MEAN`, `_MIN`, `_MAX`, `_3`), age
(`DAYS_BIRTH`), time employed (`EMPLOYED_AGE_RATIO`, `DAYS_EMPLOYED`), time
since the phone number changed (`DAYS_LAST_PHONE_CHANGE`) and the loan relative
to the goods price (`CREDIT_GOODS_RATIO`). The loan amount, income and payment
stay at the median.

```{r personas}
years <- \(y) -round(y * 365.25)

personas_raw <- bind_rows(
  "Median applicant" = median_applicant,
  Jane = median_applicant |>
    mutate(SK_ID_CURR = 1,
           EXT_SOURCE_2 = 0.70, EXT_SOURCE_3 = 0.70,
           DAYS_BIRTH = years(50), DAYS_EMPLOYED = years(12),
           DAYS_LAST_PHONE_CHANGE = years(5),
           AMT_GOODS_PRICE = AMT_CREDIT),
  Marcus = median_applicant |>
    mutate(SK_ID_CURR = 2,
           EXT_SOURCE_2 = 0.25, EXT_SOURCE_3 = 0.25,
           DAYS_BIRTH = years(26), DAYS_EMPLOYED = years(1),
           DAYS_LAST_PHONE_CHANGE = years(2 / 12),
           AMT_GOODS_PRICE = round(AMT_CREDIT / 1.25)),
  .id = "persona")

personas <- prep_env$apply_prep(select(personas_raw, -persona), prepared$params)
stopifnot(setequal(names(personas), setdiff(names(train), "TARGET")))
```

Each changed value, with the share of training applicants at or below it, a
check that each is a value real applicants hold:

```{r persona-profile}
real <- raw_train |>
  transmute(ext_2   = EXT_SOURCE_2,
            ext_3   = EXT_SOURCE_3,
            age     = -DAYS_BIRTH / 365.25,
            employed = -na_if(DAYS_EMPLOYED, 365243) / 365.25,
            phone   = -DAYS_LAST_PHONE_CHANGE / 365.25,
            credit_goods = AMT_CREDIT / AMT_GOODS_PRICE)

persona_values <- personas_raw |>
  transmute(persona,
            ext_2   = EXT_SOURCE_2,
            ext_3   = EXT_SOURCE_3,
            age     = -DAYS_BIRTH / 365.25,
            employed = -DAYS_EMPLOYED / 365.25,
            phone   = -DAYS_LAST_PHONE_CHANGE / 365.25,
            credit_goods = AMT_CREDIT / AMT_GOODS_PRICE)

field_labels <- c(ext_2 = "External score 2", ext_3 = "External score 3",
                  age = "Age (years)", employed = "Years in current job",
                  phone = "Years since phone number changed",
                  credit_goods = "Loan / price of goods")

persona_values |>
  pivot_longer(-persona, names_to = "field") |>
  mutate(percentile = map2_dbl(field, value, \(f, v) mean(real[[f]] <= v, na.rm = TRUE)),
         shown = sprintf("%s (%s)", number(value, accuracy = 0.01), percent(percentile, accuracy = 1)),
         field = field_labels[field]) |>
  select(field, persona, shown) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = persona, values_from = shown) |>
  kable(caption = "Value (share of training applicants at or below it)")
```

## Scores

The personas are scored by the final model fit on all training rows, while the
cutoffs above come from out-of-fold predictions. The two are on the same scale
if the final model's predictions for new applicants (the test set) are spread
like the out-of-fold ones:

```{r scale-check}
test_risk <- predict(final_fit, test, type = "prob")$.pred_1
probs     <- c(0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90)

rbind(`Out-of-fold (train)` = quantile(scored$model_risk, probs),
      `Final model (test)`  = quantile(test_risk, probs)) |>
  kable(digits = 4)
```

```{r persona-scores}
cutoff_5 <- at_targets$model_cutoff[at_targets$target == 0.05]

persona_scores <- tibble(
  persona = personas_raw$persona,
  predicted_default = predict(final_fit, personas, type = "prob")$.pred_1
) |>
  mutate(cutoff_at_5pct_target = cutoff_5,
         decision = if_else(predicted_default <= cutoff_5, "Approve", "Decline"))

persona_scores |>
  mutate(across(c(predicted_default, cutoff_at_5pct_target), \(x) percent(x, accuracy = 0.1))) |>
  kable()
```

At the 5% target the model approves applicants with a predicted default
probability up to `r percent(cutoff_5, accuracy = 0.1)`. The marginal applicant
carries far more risk than the 5% average, because the approved group is
mostly much safer applicants. The median applicant sits close to that line.

## Why: top 5 factors

`predcontrib = TRUE` splits each persona's prediction into one contribution per
feature, on the log-odds scale. The contributions add to the persona's
predicted log-odds of default, starting from the model's baseline for an
average applicant. `xgb_contributions()` checks that sum against the model's
own prediction before returning anything.

Several features encode the same input: age appears as `DAYS_BIRTH`,
`AGE_YEARS` and `AGE_BAND`; the external scores as each score plus their mean,
minimum, maximum and count; categories as one dummy per level. Their
contributions are added together, so each row below is one thing about the
applicant.

```{r contributions}
factor_cols <- names(select(train, where(is.factor), -TARGET))

contributions <- xgb_contributions(final_fit, personas) |>
  mutate(persona = personas_raw$persona[.row])

baseline_log_odds <- contributions |>
  filter(feature == "BIAS") |>
  pull(contribution) |>
  unique()

grouped <- contributions |>
  filter(feature != "BIAS") |>
  mutate(factor = feature_group(feature, factor_cols)) |>
  group_by(persona, factor) |>
  summarise(contribution = sum(contribution), .groups = "drop")
```

The baseline is `r number(baseline_log_odds, accuracy = 0.01)` log-odds, a
`r percent(plogis(baseline_log_odds), accuracy = 0.1)` default probability.

```{r top-factors}
#| results: asis
for (who in c("Jane", "Marcus")) {
  score <- persona_scores$predicted_default[persona_scores$persona == who]
  cat(sprintf("\n**%s**: predicted default %s (%s at the 5%% target)\n\n",
              who, percent(score, accuracy = 0.1),
              persona_scores$decision[persona_scores$persona == who]))
  grouped |>
    filter(persona == who) |>
    slice_max(abs(contribution), n = 5) |>
    transmute(rank   = row_number(),
              factor,
              effect = if_else(contribution > 0, "pushes risk up", "pushes risk down"),
              log_odds = contribution) |>
    kable(digits = 2) |>
    print()
  cat("\n")
}
```

A contribution is measured against the baseline applicant, not against the
median applicant the personas started from, so an unchanged feature can still
appear in the list.

Marcus's age pushes his risk *down*, although default falls with age overall
in the EDA. That is what the data show once the external scores are known:
among applicants with external scores as low as his, younger applicants
default no more often than middle-aged ones, so the youth effect seen overall
is already carried by the scores.

```{r age-check}
marcus_ext <- personas$EXT_SOURCE_MEAN[personas_raw$persona == "Marcus"]

train |>
  mutate(group = if_else(EXT_SOURCE_MEAN <= 0.35, "low_ext_score", "other")) |>
  group_by(AGE_BAND) |>
  summarise(all_applicants        = mean(TARGET == "1"),
            low_ext_score_default = mean(TARGET[group == "low_ext_score"] == "1"),
            low_ext_score_rows    = sum(group == "low_ext_score"),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(across(c(all_applicants, low_ext_score_default), \(x) percent(x, accuracy = 0.1))) |>
  kable(format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
        caption = sprintf("Default rate by age band; low external score = EXT_SOURCE_MEAN at or below 0.35 (Marcus: %.2f)",
                          marcus_ext))
```

# Limitations

- **Approved applicants only.** The training data holds only applicants Home
  Credit approved; those it declined, and how they would have repaid, are not
  in it (no reject inference). The approval rates here re-rank the applicants
  Home Credit already approved. They do not show what would happen to
  applicants it declined, who are likely riskier.
- **The benchmark is a stand-in.** `EXT_SOURCE_MEAN` represents underwriting on
  external scores alone. It is not Home Credit's actual approval policy, which
  is not in the data, so the gains above are measured against this stand-in,
  not against the current process.
- **`TARGET` marks payment difficulties**, not necessarily a written-off loan,
  and `AMT_CREDIT` is principal, not loss.
